passages.t: Anointed in private, and three signs
passages.happening:
At the edge of the town Samuel takes a flask of oil and pours it on Saul's head. He kisses him and says, “Has not the LORD anointed you ruler over His inheritance?” (verse 1).

Then he gives Saul three signs. At Rachel's tomb in Zelzah, two men will tell him that the donkeys have been found and that his father is now worried about him (verse 2). At the Oak of Tabor, three men going up to worship God at Bethel will meet him, carrying young goats, loaves of bread and a skin of wine, and they will give him two loaves (verses 3-4). At Gibeah of God, where the Philistines have an outpost, he will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place with harps, tambourines, flutes and lyres, prophesying (verse 5).

“Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them; and you will be transformed into a different person. When these signs have come, do as the occasion demands, for God is with you” (verses 6-7).

And one more instruction. Saul is to go to Gilgal and wait seven days for Samuel to come and offer the sacrifices and tell him what to do (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Anointing with oil was a sign of being set apart, used for priests and kings across the ancient world. In Israel it meant that God had chosen the person. Samuel's kiss was probably a sign of respect, even homage. Samuel calls Israel the LORD's inheritance: the king will rule over a people that belongs to God.

Signs like these were a common way to confirm a prophet's word. When the smaller things came true, the person could trust the larger promise.

The places mark Saul's route home through Benjamin. Rachel's tomb is set here on the border of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem, while Genesis links her burial with the road to Ephrath, which later tradition placed at Bethlehem to the south. Scholars explain the difference in more than one way: Ephrath may first have named a region near Benjamin's border, or there may have been different traditions about the site. The Oak of Tabor and Zelzah cannot be placed with certainty.

A Philistine outpost in the heart of Benjamin shows how far their control had reached into the hills. It explains why the people wanted a war leader.

Verse 8 plants a detail that will matter. Saul is to wait seven days at Gilgal for Samuel. In chapter 13 he will not wait.
passages.later:
Genesis remembers Rachel's grave on a road: ‘So Rachel died and was buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem)’ (Genesis 35:19).

The same strong verb for the Spirit rushing upon someone is used of Samson in the book of Judges, where ‘the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him’ (Judges 14:6), and it will be used of David (16:13).
passages.asks: Samuel gave Saul small signs to steady him for a large calling. Ask what small signs of God's care you have been given, and whether you have let them steady you. And ask what it would mean for you to wait, as Saul was told to wait, when you want to act.

passages.t: A changed heart, and a man among the prophets
passages.happening:
“As Saul turned to leave Samuel, God changed Saul’s heart, and all the signs came to pass that day” (verse 9).

At Gibeah a group of prophets meets him. ‘Then the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied along with them’ (verse 10). People who had known him before are astonished: “What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?” (verse 11). A man who lives there answers, “And who is their father?” (verse 12). The question becomes a saying.

When Saul's uncle asks where he has been, Saul tells him they went to Samuel about the donkeys. “He assured us that the donkeys had been found” (verse 16). ‘But Saul did not tell his uncle what Samuel had said about the kingship’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The narrator says simply that all the signs came to pass that day. That shows God standing behind Samuel's word.

The group of prophets belonged to a kind of prophetic band that appears at several points in the Old Testament. Their prophesying, with music, seems to have been a visible and shared experience, quite different from the spoken messages of later prophets like Isaiah. Music goes with prophecy elsewhere too.

The verb for the Spirit rushing upon Saul suggests something sudden and powerful, not a slow influence. In the Old Testament the Spirit often comes upon leaders to equip them for a task, as with the judges.

‘Is Saul also among the prophets?’ became a proverb. A second story of how it began comes in chapter 19, where it takes on a darker meaning. Here its tone is unclear: surprise, perhaps mockery, at seeing the ordinary son of Kish among prophets. The reply, ‘And who is their father?’, is also unclear. It may mean that the gift of prophecy does not come by family, so anyone may receive it.

Saul says nothing to his uncle about the kingship. Some read that as humility. Others read it as the first sign of the hesitation that will mark him.
passages.later:
Music and prophecy go together elsewhere. The prophet Elisha asked for a harpist, ‘And while the harpist played, the hand of the LORD came upon Elisha’ (2 Kings 3:15).

In the wilderness, when the Spirit rested on seventy elders, ‘they prophesied’ (Numbers 11:25), a sign that God had set them apart.
passages.hard:
If God changed Saul's heart and gave him the Spirit, how could Saul fail so badly later?

Saul's story is one of the Bible's sharpest puzzles about God's gifts and human responsibility. Some readers argue that the changed heart and the coming of the Spirit here equipped Saul for kingship, giving him courage and ability, without the kind of lasting inner renewal the New Testament describes. In the Old Testament the Spirit often empowered people for service, and could leave (16:14). Others think Saul did truly turn toward God, but that God's gifts do not remove human responsibility, and his later disobedience was a real turning away. Still others look at the details of this chapter, where Saul's response is already uncertain: he hides from his uncle what Samuel said, and he will hide among the baggage when he is chosen, which some read as humility and others as fear.

The chapter does not settle the question. But the rest of Saul's story shows that receiving a gift from God is no guarantee of using it faithfully.
passages.asks: God changed Saul's heart, and Saul's story still went wrong. Ask what gifts you have been given that you are not using faithfully. And ask whether you are counting on a good beginning to carry you, instead of the daily choice to obey.

passages.t: Chosen by lot, found among the baggage
passages.happening:
Samuel calls the people together before the LORD at Mizpah. He reminds them that God brought them out of Egypt and saved them from all who oppressed them. ‘But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your troubles and afflictions’ (verse 19). Then he has them come forward by tribes and clans.

The tribe of Benjamin is taken, then the clan of Matri, then Saul son of Kish. But they cannot find him (verses 20-21). They ask the LORD whether the man has come, and the LORD answers, “Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage” (verse 22).

They run and bring him, and he stands a head taller than everyone (verse 23). Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see the one the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people” (verse 24). And all the people shout, “Long live the king!”

Samuel explains to the people the rights of kingship. ‘He wrote them on a scroll and laid it up before the LORD’ (verse 25). Saul goes home to Gibeah, and men of valor ‘whose hearts God had touched’ go with him (verse 26). But some worthless men say, “How can this man save us?” They despise him and bring him no gifts, ‘but Saul remained silent about it’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Mizpah was where Israel had turned back to God and won a victory in chapter 7. Now, in the same place, Samuel tells them again that asking for a king was a rejection of God. The gift and the rebuke come together.

Choosing by lot was a way of seeking God's decision for serious matters, like dividing the land or finding a guilty person. The lot narrows from tribe to clan to man, so that everyone can see that the choice is God's and not Samuel's.

The scene has a touch of comedy. The lot falls on Saul, and the new king cannot be found. God has to tell them where he is hiding. Some read his hiding as modesty. Others read it as fear.

‘Long live the king’ was the traditional cry when a king was acclaimed.

Samuel writes the rights of kingship on a scroll and lays it before the LORD. The king is not to be an absolute ruler. He is to be a steward over a people that belongs to God, bound by a written charter, as the law of Moses had said.

The chapter ends with two groups: the valiant men whose hearts God touched, and the worthless men who despise Saul. His silence toward his critics will be tested in the next chapter.
passages.later:
The law had said that a king must keep a written copy of God's instruction: ‘It is to remain with him, and he is to read from it all the days of his life’ (Deuteronomy 17:19).

The lot that narrows from tribe to clan to man was used in Joshua's day to find the man who had stolen from Jericho (Joshua 7:14).
passages.asks: The new king hid among the baggage, and his critics asked, ‘How can this man save us?’ Ask how you respond when you are chosen for something that frightens you. And ask how you respond to those who despise you, whether with silence, revenge or something better.
